Fox Evolution:
A Demonstration Report


Simulated morphometric analysis of three fox species

Author
Affiliation

Radek Jaźwiec

Celon Pharma S.A.

Published

09-11-2026

WarningDemonstration document

This report exists only to showcase the report format (title page, headers, numbering, cross-references, landscape pages, appendices, bibliography). All data are simulated, all references are fictitious, and no result has any scientific meaning. Photographs are taken from Wikimedia Commons under the licenses stated in the captions.

1 Summary

Three fox species (red, Arctic and fennec fox) were compared on simulated morphometric data from 150 specimens collected at 6 sites and spanning the last 3.5 million years (Ma). Body mass changed by -3.4% per million years of specimen age in the red fox, and ear length increased by 0.13 cm per °C of mean annual temperature (Section 4). Lineage accumulation differed between three fictional clades (Figure 5). The description is exploratory and purely illustrative.

2 Introduction

2.1 Background

Foxes are small to medium-sized members of the family Canidae and occupy habitats from Arctic tundra to hot desert [1]. Their appendages are a textbook illustration of adaptation to ambient temperature: large ears in the fennec fox dissipate heat, whereas the compact ears of the Arctic fox conserve it [2]. Figure 1 shows a historical painting of common foxes in a winter landscape.

2.2 Objectives

The objectives of this demonstration analysis were to

  1. describe the change of body mass over geological time,
  2. relate ear length to mean annual temperature, and
  3. compare the accumulation of lineages between clades.

3 Methods

3.1 Specimens and data sources

Specimen records were simulated for three species (Table 1). Each record holds the site, the specimen age, the mean annual temperature at the site and time of deposition, and five morphometric measurements1. Sampling bias is a known problem of fossil data [3] and is ignored here.

3.2 Statistical analysis

Body mass \(m\) of specimen \(j\) of species \(s\) was modeled on the log scale as a linear function of specimen age \(t\),

\[ \log m_{sj} = \beta_{0,s} + \beta_{1,s}\, t_{sj} + \varepsilon_{sj}, \qquad \varepsilon_{sj} \sim N(0, \sigma^2), \tag{1}\]

and ear length was modeled analogously on mean annual temperature. Both models contain a species-specific intercept and slope (details in Section 8). Lineages through time were simulated as a pure-birth process [4]. Skull shape scores were derived as described by [5].

Note

All p-values are descriptive. No hypothesis was specified in advance, so no multiplicity adjustment was made.

4 Results

4.1 Body mass through time

Body mass was highest in the red fox and lowest in the fennec fox, with a slight increase towards the present in all three species (Figure 2). On the log scale the red fox slope was -0.035 per million years (Table 3).

4.2 Ear size and climate

Ear length increased with mean annual temperature in every species (Figure 3), in line with the heat-dissipation argument of [2]. The fennec fox (Figure 4) had the longest ears at every temperature.

4.3 Diversification

The three fictional clades accumulated lineages at different rates (Figure 5). Clade I, the fastest, accumulated the most lineages, whereas Clade III grew only modestly.

4.4 Specimen-level data

Table 2 lists a selection of specimens with all measurements. The table occupies a full landscape page; the page orientation returns to portrait after it.

5 Discussion

The simulated data reproduce the qualitative pattern expected from the literature: larger bodies in the temperate species, and longer ears in warmer climates. The effect sizes carry no information because the data were generated from the same equations that were used to analyze them.

5.1 Limitations

  • The data are fictional.
  • Specimen age was drawn independently of site, so no spatial structure exists.
  • The lineage process ignores extinction.
